content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Karen Alexander (E030) requests write access to Source Code.

The team notes:
- Notes 1-5 (HR, IT, Finance, Compliance, Facilities) say she is a full-time Analyst. Full-time employees can have up to write (admin only if role owns system, which is Engineer, not Analyst). So write is allowed.
- Note 6 (Security) says she is a contractor with basic security training (not advanced). Per policy, contractors may have read, or write only with advanced security training; never admin. Requested write exceeds maximum of read, so recommend read.

Conflict: One note (Security) says contractor with basic training, while others say full-time. The Security DB is the one that handles security training. Hmm.

The policy: contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

If she is full-time, max is write for Analyst (up to write). Requested write = grant write.

If she is contractor with basic training, max is read. Requested write exceeds max, grant read.

Which to believe? The security note is one source. The other five say full-time. Hmm, but the Security DB might be the authority on employment type? Actually HR is typically the authority on employment type. The notes 1-5 all say full-time Analyst. Note 6 says contractor with basic security training.

Since most notes say full-time, and the policy for full-time allows write, and requested is write, grant write.

However, the conflicting security note creates ambiguity. Let me think about how the team typically resolves this. Notes stay in shared memory. The Approver reads the notes and makes final decision.

Given there are 5 notes confirming full-time Analyst and 1 note claiming contractor, the majority evidence is full-time. Under the policy, full-time employees may have up to write (admin only if role owns system - Analyst doesn't own Source Code, Engineer does). Requested write is at the maximum, so grant write.

I'll go with write.

Let me submit the decision.
